pharm: Bactericidal beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and resists staphylococcal penicillinase, giving activity against penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus aureus
quick: 125 mg every 6 h (mild-moderate); 250 mg every 6 h (severe)
Take on empty stomach 1 h before or 2 h after food, with plenty of water
Use only if clearly needed; no evidence of fetal harm but limited controlled data
Excreted in breast milk; use with caution
Largely renally excreted but short half-life; no major adjustment usually needed
Partly hepatically inactivated; use with usual caution
Clinical response; INR if on warfarin; watch for hypersensitivity and C. difficile
summary: Dicloxacillin is an oral isoxazolyl, penicillinase-resistant (anti-staphylococcal) penicillin that is bactericidal by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It is indicated for infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci shown to be susceptible (methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, MSSA) - typically skin and soft-tissue infections. The usual adult dose is 125 mg every 6 hours for mild-to-moderate infection and 250 mg every 6 hours for severe infection; children under 40 kg receive 12.5-25 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 6 hours. It is acid-stable but incompletely absorbed and must be taken on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) with adequate water, not lying down, to avoid oesophageal irritation. Penicillinase-resistant penicillins should not replace penicillin G for penicillin-susceptible organisms. Serious, occasionally fatal anaphylaxis can occur, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea has been reported.
indications: Infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci demonstrated to be susceptible to dicloxacillin (e.g. methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus)
Empiric initiation of therapy in suspected resistant (penicillinase-producing) staphylococcal infection pending culture results
Commonly used for skin and soft-tissue infections, and as oral step-down from parenteral anti-staphylococcal therapy

dosage.n: Confirm susceptibility; not for penicillin-G-susceptible organisms
Oral therapy not for initial treatment of serious life-threatening infections

dosage.c: Children under 40 kg - mild to moderate
dosage.d: 12.5 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 6 hours
25 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 6 hours
dosage.n: Children over 40 kg use adult doses

admin: Take on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals - food delays and reduces absorption
Swallow with at least 120 mL (4 fl oz) of water and do not take lying down or immediately before bed (risk of oesophageal burning/ulceration)
Obtain a thorough drug and allergy history (penicillin/cephalosporin allergy) before starting
Perform cultures and susceptibility tests; do not continue a penicillinase-resistant penicillin if the organism is penicillin-G-susceptible
Do not mix in vitro with aminoglycosides (mutual inactivation)
Probenecid co-administration increases and prolongs serum levels if higher levels are required
moa: Dicloxacillin is a semisynthetic, acid-stable, penicillinase-resistant penicillin of the isoxazolyl series. Like all beta-lactams it binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits the transpeptidation step of bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect against actively dividing organisms. Bulky side chains sterically protect the beta-lactam ring from staphylococcal penicillinase (beta-lactamase), so it retains activity against penicillinase-producing staphylococci that destroy penicillin G. It is not active against methicillin-resistant staphylococci.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dicloxacillin, any penicillin, or any component of the formulation
relative: History of significant allergy or asthma
Use as monotherapy in serious life-threatening infection (oral route inadequate)
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity, especially early in therapy
Diarrhoea suggestive of C. difficile colitis
INR in patients on warfarin (dicloxacillin may reduce anticoagulant response)
Renal/hepatic/haematologic function on prolonged high-dose therapy

preg: Animal reproduction studies with penicillinase-resistant penicillins have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or fetal harm, and human experience with penicillins has not shown clear adverse fetal effects, but adequate well-controlled studies are lacking. Use dicloxacillin in pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Penicillins are excreted into breast milk. Caution should be exercised when dicloxacillin is given to a nursing mother; monitor the infant for sensitisation, diarrhoea or candidiasis.
renal: Dicloxacillin is rapidly excreted, mainly unchanged in the urine, but has a very short half-life (about 0.7 hour) and nonrenal (hepatic/biliary) elimination also contributes; significant dose adjustment is generally not required in renal impairment. It is not appreciably removed by dialysis.
hepatic: A portion of dicloxacillin is inactivated hepatically and excreted in bile. Use with the usual caution in hepatic impairment; rare hepatic enzyme elevations and cholestasis have been reported with anti-staphylococcal penicillins.

major: Warfarin/dicoumarol - dicloxacillin may reduce the anticoagulant response (possible hepatic enzyme induction); monitor INR and adjust dose
moderate: Probenecid - increases and prolongs serum penicillin levels by reducing renal tubular secretion
Tetracyclines and other bacteriostatic agents - may antagonise the bactericidal action of penicillins; avoid combination
Aminoglycosides - physically/chemically incompatible in vitro; administer separately and do not mix
minor: May reduce efficacy of combined oral contraceptives (theoretical)
interactions.food: Food markedly reduces and delays absorption - take on an empty stomach
interactions.diagnostics: Penicillins can falsely lower serum aminoglycoside assay results in co-treated patients; may cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests

serious: Anaphylaxis and other immediate hypersensitivity reactions (can be fatal)
Serum sickness-like delayed reactions (fever, urticaria, arthralgia)
Oesophageal ulceration if taken with insufficient water or before lying down
rare: Haematologic effects - neutropenia, eosinophilia, haemolytic anaemia
Neurotoxicity (seizures) with very high doses or accumulation

monitoring: Clinical response and resolution of infection
Signs of hypersensitivity, especially during the first doses
Renal, hepatic and haematologic parameters during prolonged or high-dose therapy
counsel: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water and stay upright; do not take it just before lying down
Take the full course even if you feel better, and at evenly spaced times
Tell your doctor about any previous reaction to penicillin or other antibiotics before starting
Stop the medicine and seek urgent help for rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing
Report watery or bloody diarrhoea, which can occur even weeks after finishing
Antibiotics do not treat viral illnesses such as colds
pk: Rapid bactericidal action; absorption rapid but incomplete
Peak serum levels in about 1 to 1.5 hours (10-17 mcg/mL after a 500 mg dose)
Store capsules at controlled room temperature in a tightly closed container
pearls: Penicillinase-resistant (anti-staphylococcal) penicillin - first-line oral option for MSSA, especially skin/soft-tissue infection
No activity against MRSA, enterococci, or gram-negative organisms
Must be taken on an empty stomach with water and upright to avoid oesophageal ulceration
Highly protein-bound (~98%) with a very short half-life - dose every 6 hours
Can reduce the effect of warfarin - monitor INR
Not for serious life-threatening infections as initial therapy - use parenteral agents first
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose - do not double up. Space the remaining doses evenly and complete the full course.
overdose: Overdose may cause gastrointestinal upset and, with very high concentrations (especially in renal impairment), neurotoxicity such as seizures. Treatment is supportive; discontinue the drug and manage symptomatically. Dicloxacillin is not appreciably removed by haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
